task.pr_title: Improve error boundary handling for unmounted subtrees

cases.provenance: A human reviewer flagged this defect in an inline comment on the reviewed pull request.
cases.description: The nearestMountedAncestor is by definition a parent of the thing that threw. So why are we starting by checking one level above that? It seems to me that this would target the wrong ancestor if the thing being deleted is a direct child of the error boundary itself. Your tests doesn't seem to test this case because they all use the `Conditional` wrapper.

evidence.thread_resolution:
bvaughn: > The nearestMountedAncestor is by definition a parent of the thing that threw.

No? It's not necessarily the root of the unmounted tree. We traverse that subtree for effects– so the thing that threw may be further down inside of the unmounted tree.

> So why are we starting by checking one level above that?

I don't understand what you're suggesting. We've already disconnected the `return` pointer at this point (after layout). This is the mechanism we rely on for detecting and ignoring (and warning about) an unmounted state update. We need to jump *out* of the unmounted tree back to the mounted tree so that (a) we're calling a still-mounted boundary and (b) anything we attempt to update will actually be scheduled (since trying to schedule an updated on an also-unmounted boundary wouldn't do anything).

Am I misunderstanding you somehow?

> Your tests doesn't seem to test this case because they all use the `Conditional` wrapper.

I'm not sure I understand the case you think my tests are missing. Maybe I'm just not fully awake yet.
bvaughn: Oh, I think I get what you're saying. You're sound the "nearest mounted ancestor" is *already* an ancestor, so starting with `.return` is wrong. I gotcha. The "parent" comment threw me off.

Yeah, that's an accident.

I'll add a test case that would fail (and a fix).
